summary:
New South Wales stands under the Australian national framework. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, effective immediately) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment.

State-level vilification coverage is narrower than in several other Australian jurisdictions. New South Wales, the Australian Capital Territory and Victoria cover only sexual orientation, while South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland also name gender identity and the Northern Territory and Western Australia name neither. A trans visitor in New South Wales therefore retains federal discrimination remedies, including the Tickle v Giggle precedent, but has no state vilification ground specific to gender identity.

The Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 took effect on 4 April 2025. Practices causing substantial mental or physical harm are punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, taking a person out of New South Wales for conversion therapy carries up to three years, and Anti-Discrimination NSW can investigate complaints from 4 April 2025 with civil referral pathways available. The state's other principal recent instrument is the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024.

Trans visitors have been killed in the state. In July 2021 ABC Background Briefing reported the investigation into the killing of Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old transgender woman from the Philippines who was visiting Australia, in Wagga Wagga; the perpetrator's guilty plea to manslaughter drew a 22-month term, a custodial outcome far below a murder sentence.

The restrictive machinery reported elsewhere in Australia does not apply here: no law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers entering New South Wales or Australia, and marriage equality has held since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017. Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and overseas same-sex marriages are recognised automatically.

Care access for young people rests on state-commissioned evidence: a New South Wales independent review released in September 2024 found puberty blockers safe, effective and reversible while calling for more long-term research. That review stands in contrast to the restrictions operating in Queensland public health services.
tangentialFactors:
Protection varies sharply across the country, which matters for onward travel. Victoria's Anti-vilification Act 2025 carries gender identity as a ground and takes effect on 30 June 2026; Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections for gender-diverse people in April 2024. Queensland's January 2025 pause on new puberty blocker and cross-sex hormone prescriptions for under-18s in public health services was ruled unlawful by the Queensland Supreme Court on 27 October 2025, then reinstated substantially by a new ministerial directive on 28 October 2025 pending reviews, with a legal challenge filed in December 2025. A trans traveller with a minor crossing into Queensland should expect a different care environment than the one described for New South Wales.

Detention policy elsewhere in the country offers a comparison point. Queensland's inspection standards of August 2023, issued under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, but staff retain discretion at admission and transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that identity-based process; the 2009 Corrective Services procedure they replaced was assessed as largely ineffective. Equivalent New South Wales correctional guidance is not covered by the sources held here.

The Tickle v Giggle ruling of August 2024 was reported by Reuters as a landmark for gender-identity discrimination, and because it turns on federal law it applies nationally rather than only in New South Wales.

Residents face a state vilification law that lists sexual orientation but not gender identity, so vilification complaints framed on gender-identity grounds must be brought federally. Anti-discrimination complaints on gender-identity grounds proceed under the federal Sex Discrimination Act as interpreted in Tickle v Giggle.

Local service policy draws on the New South Wales independent review of September 2024, which characterised puberty blockers as safe, effective and reversible while recommending further long-term research, giving the state's public health position a documented evidentiary basis.
outOfScopeNotes:
The New South Wales Parliament bill document for the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024 would not load, so the specific provisions of that Act rest on the record held here rather than on a live parliamentary page; the substance of its amendments is unresolved against a primary source.

The Queensland Human Rights Commission announcement underpinning that state's April 2024 strengthening of protections is no longer reachable and is cited in this dossier from the retained record only.

No source in the inventory addresses how New South Wales correctional authorities decide placement of trans prisoners, whether any state facility applies a lived-gender rule, or what inspection oversight applies. Whether New South Wales has experienced border or airport screening incidents involving trans travellers is likewise not sourced; the absence of reported friction is not evidence of a formal policy.

Enforcement data for the federal hate-crime provisions of February 2025 in New South Wales, and any prosecution history under the Conversion Practices Ban Act since April 2025, are not covered by the sources held here.
